# Neoadjuvant intent anti-programmed death-1 immunotherapy for cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma in patients with hematologic malignancy

**Authors:** Kyle Murchison; Karam Khaddour; Anthony Camargo; Emily Ruiz; Rosh Sethi; Eleni Rettig; Charles Yoon; Emily Y Kim; Mia DeSimone; Justine Cohen; Nicole R LeBoeuf; Nina Ran; Manisha Thakuria; Ann W Silk

**Affiliations:** Department of Medicine, Florida Atlantic University Charles E. Schmidt College of Medicine, Boca Raton, FL, 33431, United States | Department of Dermatology, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA, 02215, United States | Division of Hematology and Oncology, Department of Medicine,Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, 02215, United States | Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, 02215, United States | University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA, 01655, United States | University of Michigan, Department of Dermatology, Ann Arbor, MI, 48109, United States

## Abstract

Patients with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC) and concurrent hematologic malignancy are underrepresented in clinical trials of anti-programmed death-1 (PD1) therapy due to concerns about efficacy and safety. The objective of this study is to evaluate clinical outcomes and safety of neoadjuvant anti-PD1 in patients with CSCC and concurrent hematologic malignancy.

This is a retrospective single-institution cohort study of neoadjuvant-intent anti-PD-1 therapy in patients with advanced CSCC and a concurrent hematologic malignancy. Patient and tumor characteristics are described. Clinical and pathologic response to anti-PD-1 therapy, safety, and CSCC recurrence risk and disease-specific survival are reported.

Ten patients with CSCC and a concurrent hematologic malignancy received immunotherapy with neoadjuvant intent. All patients were treated with cemiplimab, and 4/10 patients experienced a response by composite assessment of clinical, radiographic, and pathologic data. Two of eight patients who underwent planned surgical resection had a complete pathologic response, and 2 of 2 patients who did not undergo surgery had a clinical response on radiographic/clinical assessment. Three patients were receiving active treatment for hematologic malignancy during immunotherapy; of these, one demonstrated a clinical and pathologic response. One patient experienced a grade 3 immune-related adverse event (arthritis).

The results suggest that anti-PD-1 therapy in the neoadjuvant setting in patients with CSCC and with concurrent hematologic malignancy is feasible. The clinical outcomes observed in this small cohort highlight the need for prospective studies of patients with concurrent hematologic malignancy in future neoadjuvant CSCC trials.

## Introduction

Recent data demonstrate the impressive efficacy of neoadjuvant immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) prior to surgery in immunocompetent patients with cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC). In a multisite clinical trial of 79 patients who received up to four doses of cemiplimab, the pathological response rate was 64% (51% complete + 13% major) among patients undergoing surgery.1 In the nivolumab arm of the MATISSE trial, a complete or major pathologic response (mPR) was seen in 9 of 20 patients (45%, including 25% complete + 20% near-complete).2 Additionally, a complete clinical response was seen in 5 of 6 patients who chose not to have surgery, resulting in a composite (clinical + pathologic) response rate of 14 of 26 patients (54%).

Despite CSCC being more aggressive in patients with hematologic malignancy and associating with high morbidity and mortality,3,4 such patients who have chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) or lymphomas were excluded from neoadjuvant trials. Therefore, there are limited data on the safety and efficacy of neoadjuvant ICI in this patient population.5 Here, we describe safety and outcomes in 10 patients with CSCC and concurrent hematologic malignancy who received antiprogrammed-death-1 (anti-PD-1) therapy with neoadjuvant intent.

## Methods

A retrospective study was performed of patients with CSCC and a concurrent hematologic malignancy at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute who received neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 for advanced resectable CSCC between October 2021 and September 2024. The study was approved by IRB (DF/HCC #24-516). Patients who had active hematologic malignancy were included whether they were on active treatment or not. Neoadjuvant intent was defined as the administration of ICI before a planned surgery. Patients who ultimately did not proceed to surgery were included in the analysis. We reviewed patient and tumor characteristics, treatment, clinical, radiologic and pathologic response, immune-related adverse events (irAEs), recurrence, and disease-specific survival. Clinical response was defined as visible or palpable tumor shrinkage or regression on physical examination and/or reduced size on imaging, according to radiology reports. Pathologic response was classified as complete pathologic response (pCR; no viable tumor), mPR(≤10% viable tumor), or no pathologic response (pNR; >10% viable tumor) by a board-certified dermatopathologist.

## Results

Ten patients were identified, and their characteristics and outcomes are described in Table 1. Seven (70%) had CLL and three (30%) had other lymphomas. The median age was 78 years (range 61-89), most patients were male (n = 9, 90%) and had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance score of 1 (n = 7, 70%); the remaining had scores of 0 (n = 2, 20%) and 2 (n = 1, 10%). The most common location for CSCC was the head and neck (n = 8, 80%), with one tumor located on the trunk and one on the extremity. At the time of neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy, most patients had stage IV (n = 6, 60%) and the remaining had stage III (n = 3, 30%) and stage I (n = 1, 10%) according to AJCC, 8th edition. All patients received cemiplimab, and 8 underwent surgery (Figure 1). Patients received a median of 2 cycles (range, 1-5) prior to surgery.

Based on a combined assessment of clinical, radiographic, and pathologic data, a composite response was observed in 4 of 10 patients, and response by physical exam was documented in all 4 cases. Among patients who had radiographic assessment, 2 of 7 had a partial response. Among the 8 patients who underwent surgery, 2 of 8 had pCR and 6 of 8 had pNR. One patient died unexpectedly prior to radiologic evaluation and surgery, though physical examination showed clinical response (Figure S1). Three patients were receiving treatment for hematologic malignancy during neoadjuvant immunotherapy, two with a combination of anti-CD20 antibody and B-cell lymphoma 2 therapy, and one with a Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor. One of these 3 patients had a clinical and pathologic response.

At a median follow-up of 25 months (range, 2-42 months), 2 patients had CSCC recurrence, 1 with osseous metastasis and 1 with nodal metastasis, while 7 remained disease-free. Six patients had irAEs of any grade, including 1 who required systemic corticosteroids for grade 3 arthritis. One patient experienced a grade 2 infusion reaction to cemiplimab, resulting in permanent discontinuation of cemiplimab.

## Discussion

This retrospective study of 10 patients provides preliminary data on the safety and efficacy of neoadjuvant immunotherapy in patients with CSCC who suffer from concurrent hematologic malignancies. The frequency of grade ≥3 irAEs was (10%), which is comparable to studies of patients with concomitant hematologic malignancies receiving anti-PD-1,4 suggesting an acceptable safety profile in these high-risk patients. The frequency of response by either pathologic or clinical criteria was observed in 4 of 10 patients. Specifically, we observed a pCR in 2 of 8 evaluable (surgical) patients, and a clinical response in 2 of 2 non-surgical patients.

The efficacy outcomes we observed are comparable to the clinical benefit rates reported in immunocompetent patients. In the multisite cemiplimab neoadjuvant study by Gross et al., 9 patients (11%) did not undergo surgery in the protocol-specified window and therefore had no pathological evaluation. The pCR rate for this study was 51% in those who underwent surgery.1 In the MATISSE study, responding patients were given the option to forgo surgery, which may have negatively impacted the pathologic response rates. Of the patients who did undergo surgery following nivolumab monotherapy, the pCR rate was 25% (5 of 20).2 Our cohort was similar to the MATISSE trial population in that the rate of pCR may have been higher if all patients would have undergone surgery. For this reason, the MATISSE study and the current study reported outcomes for the entire population as a composite response rate, which was 14 of 26 (54%) patients in the nivolumab monotherapy arm of the MATISSE study, and 4 of 10 in our study in CSCC patients with concurrent lymphoma who were treated with cemiplimab.

Patients with hematologic malignancies often exhibit immune dysfunction, including T-cell exhaustion, impaired antigen presentation, and hypogammaglobulinemia,5 which may limit responses and could provide a second explanation for the lower pCR compared to immunocompetent patients in the Gross et al. study. Concurrent treatment of hematologic malignancy with drugs that target CD20 and BTK can further modulate the tumor microenvironment and suppress immune cells. Notably, 3 of the 4 responding patients were not actively undergoing treatment for hematologic malignancy, suggesting that such therapies may hinder robust response to ICI. The 4 responders included 2 patients with untreated CLL and a patient with newly diagnosed and untreated DLBCL, reflecting the activity of cemiplimab in patients with relatively preserved immune systems. This finding suggests that optimizing immune status in patients with hematologic malignancies by discontinuing immunosuppressive therapies and targeted therapies, when possible, may improve outcomes for this cohort.

This study is limited by a small sample size and retrospective design. Nonetheless, the data underscore the importance of prospective studies in patients with hematologic malignancies. Several patients in our cohort harbored high-risk genomic alterations related to their hematologic malignancies, including TP53 mutation, 17p deletions, and unmutated immunoglobulin heavy chain variable regions, which are associated with poorer outcomes.6,7 While our study was not powered to assess associations between molecular alterations and treatment response, future research should explore whether these alterations influence response to ICI.8

In conclusion, neoadjuvant cemiplimab is feasible in patients with cSCC and concurrent hematologic malignancy, especially those not receiving other antineoplastic therapy. Moreover, in this cohort of patients, neoadjuvant cemiplimab led to clinical responses approaching those which are observed in immunocompetent patients.

However, prospective trials focused on patients with cSCC and coexisting hematologic malignancies are needed to determine which patients should be treated with neoadjuvant immunotherapy versus immediate surgical treatment.
